<reflection>
- The fitting results from the first experiment show that all 20 candidate mechanisms have very similar negative log-likelihood (NLL) values (ranging from -24.77 to -22.03). This indicates that a single progress curve under standard conditions is insufficient to distinguish the models, as they can all adjust their parameters to mimic a simple Michaelis-Menten-like profile.
- My aim for the first turn was to establish a baseline, which was achieved, but it confirms the need to perturb the system significantly to break the parameter degeneracy.
- The aim for this turn is to introduce initial product and alter the substrate-to-catalyst ratio to force the models to diverge based on their specific structural differences (e.g., product inhibition, substrate deactivation, catalyst order).
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
By introducing a high initial concentration of product (P = 0.5), we can strongly differentiate mechanisms that involve product-induced deactivation or product inhibition (M12, M17, M5) from those that do not. Furthermore, by significantly increasing the initial substrate concentration (S = 4.0) and decreasing the catalyst concentration (cat = 0.02) compared to the first experiment, we drastically change the substrate-to-catalyst ratio. This shift will alter the steady-state distribution of free catalyst versus the catalyst-substrate complex, thereby exposing differences between substrate-induced deactivation (M11, M16), substrate inhibition (M7), and higher-order catalyst interactions (M2, M3, M13, M18, M19). This combined perturbation is designed to be informative across multiple mechanistic classes simultaneously.
</hypothesis>
